section.title: The Resurrection and Ascension
section.sectionRationale: The tomb is empty. Women come at dawn with spices and find the stone rolled away and a messenger announcing that Jesus the crucified has risen and goes ahead of them to Galilee. In the Gospel's ending as printed, the risen Jesus appears, rebukes unbelief, commissions His disciples to preach the gospel to all creation, and is taken up to God's right hand, while they go out and preach everywhere with the Lord confirming His word.
section.thesis: The crucified Jesus has risen exactly as He said, vindicated by God and going ahead of His failing disciples in grace; and the risen, ascended Lord sends His people into all the world with the gospel, working with them to confirm His word.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the women at the empty tomb and the announcement of the resurrection; the risen Jesus appearing and rebuking unbelief; and the Great Commission and the ascension.

units.label: The empty tomb
units.note: He has risen, He is not here

verses.text: When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus.
Very early on the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they went to the tomb.
They were asking one another, “Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?”
But when they looked up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, even though it was extremely large.
When they entered the tomb, they saw a young man dressed in a white robe sitting on the right side, and they were alarmed.
But he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has {{egeiro|risen}}! He is not here! See the place where they put Him.
But go, tell His disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him, just as He told you.’”
So the women left the tomb and ran away, trembling and bewildered. And in their fear they did not say a word to anyone.
Early on the first day of the week, after Jesus had risen, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had driven out seven demons.
She went and told those who had been with Him, who were mourning and weeping.
And when they heard that Jesus was alive and she had seen Him, they did not believe it.
After this, Jesus appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked along in the country.
And they went back and reported it to the rest, but they did not believe them either.
Later, as they were eating, Jesus appeared to the Eleven and rebuked them for their {{apistia|unbelief}} and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen.

units.label: The Great Commission and the Ascension
units.note: go into all the world and preach the gospel

verses.text: And He said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the {{euangelion|gospel}} to every creature.
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
And these signs will accompany those who believe: In My name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues;
they will pick up snakes with their hands, and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not harm them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be made well.”
After the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, He was {{analambano|taken up}} into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.
And they went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.

egeiro.gloss: To raise, to rise. The messenger's word, He has risen, is in the passive, He has been raised, pointing to God's mighty act of raising Jesus from the dead. The resurrection is God's vindication of His crucified Son and the guarantee of His people's hope.

apistia.gloss: Unbelief, failure to trust. The risen Jesus rebukes His disciples' stubborn refusal to believe the reports of His resurrection. Their slowness underscores that faith in the risen Lord rests on real testimony, and that even the first witnesses had to be moved from unbelief to faith.

euangelion.gloss: Good news, gospel, the word that opened Mark's book. The risen Jesus sends His disciples to preach this same gospel, the announcement of His death and resurrection, to all the world, so that the story that began as the good news of Jesus now goes out to every creature.

analambano.gloss: To take up, receive up. Jesus is taken up into heaven and seated at God's right hand, the place of authority and rule. The ascension completes His exaltation: the crucified and risen One now reigns, and from there He works with His people as they preach.

basic.context: After the Sabbath, three women come to the tomb at dawn with spices, worrying about the heavy stone, only to find it already rolled away. Inside, a young man in white tells them not to be alarmed: Jesus the crucified has risen and is not there. They are to tell the disciples, and Peter by name, that He is going ahead of them to Galilee. The women flee, trembling. In the Gospel's ending as printed, the risen Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, then to two disciples, then to the Eleven, rebuking their unbelief. He commissions them to go into all the world and preach the gospel, promising that signs will accompany believers. Then He is taken up to heaven and seated at God's right hand, and the disciples go out and preach everywhere, the Lord confirming His word.
basic.hermeneutics: The resurrection is God's great reversal: the crucified is risen, exactly as Jesus foretold. The message that He goes ahead to Galilee, and the personal mention of Peter, shows grace toward the disciples who failed. The commission turns the whole Gospel outward: the good news must now reach every creature. Note honestly that the earliest manuscripts end at verse 8, and that verses 9 to 20 raise a genuine textual question, addressed in the notes.
basic.originalLanguages: The angelic word is egeiro, He has been raised, God's act on the crucified Jesus. The risen Lord rebukes the disciples' apistia, unbelief, and sends them to preach the euangelion, the gospel, before He is analambano, taken up, to God's right hand.
basic.typology: The empty tomb and resurrection fulfil Jesus' own repeated predictions and the pattern of the vindicated sufferer. The ascension to God's right hand fulfils Psalm 110, and the mission to all nations fulfils the promise that blessing would reach the whole world.
basic.christ: Jesus is the crucified and risen Lord, vindicated by God, who goes ahead of His failing disciples in grace, commissions them, and reigns from God's right hand.
basic.god: God raises Jesus from the dead, vindicating His Son and His saving work. God sends the gospel to all creation and works with His witnesses to confirm His word.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 110 gives the enthronement at God's right hand. Isaiah 49 promises salvation to the ends of the earth. Matthew 28 parallels the commission.
basic.oneStory: The story that ran from a fall in a garden to a cross now bursts open at an empty tomb. Death is undone, the crucified King is risen and enthroned, and the good news goes out to every creature. Mark's Gospel ends not as a closed account but as an open commission: the risen Lord reigns, and His people are sent to tell the world.

context.literary:
Mark 16 has two halves that read like two different books, and the BSB footnote says why. 'Early manuscripts end the Gospel of Mark after verse 8.' Verses 1 to 8 are written in Mark's own stripped, hurried style. Verses 9 to 20 read like a digest of appearances found in the other Gospels and Acts. Any honest study has to hold the two halves apart and say what each does.

Verses 1 to 8 are a small drama in three movements. The women set out with a worry, 'Who will roll away the stone?' verse 3; they arrive to find the worry removed, verse 4; and they receive a message and flee, verses 5 to 8. The scene is full of the language of astonishment. Mark has used fear and amazement as the usual response to Jesus all through the Gospel, after the stilling of the storm, Mark 4:41, and after the raising of Jairus' daughter, Mark 5:42. Here the same reaction meets the greatest of the signs.

The announcement of verse 6 is built with care. First comes the identification: 'Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified,' a phrase that keeps the cross inside the resurrection. Then the three short clauses: 'He has risen! He is not here! See the place where they put Him.' The proof offered is an empty place, and the stone that was 'extremely large' sits there rolled away.

The ending in verse 8 is deliberately abrupt. Mark ends with trembling and fear, and the last word in Greek is the little connecting word 'for.' Whether he meant to end there or the original ending was lost is the major question of the chapter. Either way, the movement of the Gospel is clear: the one who appears to be defeated is already ahead of the disciples, and the response is left to the reader.
context.historical:
The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday, so the women could buy spices only after it, and went to the tomb at first light on the first day of the week, verses 1 and 2. They meant to anoint a body that Joseph of Arimathea had wrapped in haste on Friday evening, Mark 15:42-46. Burial customs in Jerusalem of the period often used rock cut family tombs, closed with a stone, with the body laid on a ledge and spices used for the sake of respect and against the smell. The women's plan shows they expected to find a corpse, not a risen Lord.

It is worth noting who carries the story. In much of the ancient world a woman's testimony counted for little in formal settings, and a writer inventing a resurrection story for his own side would not naturally have chosen women as the first witnesses. Mark names them, and Mark names them on purpose, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome, the same three who had watched from a distance at the cross, Mark 15:40.

The apostolic preaching shows how fast the proclamation took hold. Paul, writing in the 50s, hands on as 'of first importance' that Christ was buried and raised on the third day, and lists who saw Him, including more than five hundred at once, most still alive, 1 Corinthians 15:3-8. Peter in Jerusalem a few weeks later says God raised Jesus and 'we are all witnesses,' Acts 2:32.

The long ending, verses 9 to 20, belongs to the question of how the text was handed down. The two oldest great manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, stop at verse 8, and Eusebius and Jerome in the fourth century knew that many good copies lacked what follows. Yet a longer ending was widely read in the second century, and was copied in most later manuscripts. Some copies carry a short ending instead, and the BSB gives it in a footnote. The church has long received the longer ending as Scripture while recognising that its place in the earliest text is doubtful.
context.canonical:
Jesus had said it before, and Mark has stored the sayings in advance. After the transfiguration He told three disciples not to speak 'until the Son of Man had risen from the dead,' and they discussed 'what it meant to rise from the dead,' Mark 9:9-10. Three times He announced that the Son of Man would be killed and after three days rise, Mark 8:31, 9:31 and 10:34. At the Last Supper He promised to go ahead into Galilee, Mark 14:28. The angel's words in 16:7, 'just as He told you,' tie the empty tomb to every one of those promises.

The Old Testament had prepared the ground in poetry and promise. Hosea 6:2 speaks of being raised up 'on the third day.' Psalm 16:10 says the LORD will not abandon His holy one to Sheol or let Him 'see decay,' a text Peter applies to Jesus in Acts 2:25-31. Isaiah 53:10-11 promises that the servant who is crushed will 'see the light of life' and 'prolong His days.' The ascension and enthronement of verse 19 echo Psalm 110:1, which Jesus Himself quoted in Mark 12:36 and which He tied to the Son of Man in Mark 14:62.

In the New Testament the resurrection becomes the basis of everything. Paul says that if Christ is not raised, 'your faith is futile; you are still in your sins,' 1 Corinthians 15:17, and that He was 'declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' Romans 1:4. Peter's first sermon rests on it, Acts 2:24-36. Luke and Matthew give fuller accounts of the appearances and the commission, Luke 24 and Matthew 28:16-20, and John records Mary Magdalene's meeting with the risen Lord at the tomb, John 20:11-18. The ascension is told again in Acts 1:9-11, and Hebrews returns to the enthroned Priest, Hebrews 1:3 and 10:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
If verse 8 is where Mark stopped, then he meant to leave his reader standing at the open tomb with the women, afraid, with the angel's message ringing and nobody yet obeying it. That is not a failure of nerve. Mark has shown, from the first chapter, that fear and failure are the usual human response to Jesus, and he now turns the question outward: what will you do with this word? The command to 'go, tell His disciples and Peter' is addressed to the women, but it is also spoken to every reader.

Mark also meant to give the failed disciples a reason for hope. They had run away, and Peter had denied Him three times, Mark 14:66-72. The message of verse 7 names Peter, as if to say that the one who denied Him is not struck from the list. The Shepherd who was struck and whose sheep were scattered, Mark 14:27, is going ahead of them, and the meeting He promised still stands.

He meant, further, to leave no doubt about identity. The one who is raised is 'Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified.' The resurrection does not cancel the cross or make it a mistake. It is the vindication of the cross as God's own work, and it is the proof that the claim of Mark 1:1, that He is the Son of God, was true.

For the longer ending, if it is taken as the church's later and canonical summary, its aim is to say the same things in the language of the other accounts: He is alive, His own disciples were slow to believe, He sent them, and He reigns.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1 to 8 are narrative. The women's flight and silence are recorded, not commended. Mark wants the reader to feel the weight of fear and then to see that the message must be told in spite of it, so the disobedience is a warning, not a model.

The commission of verses 15 and 16 is a command and carries to the church in every age, as the parallels in Matthew 28:19-20 and Luke 24:47 show. The promise that unbelief brings condemnation is stated as a warning, not as a rule that baptism is the only mark of faith; the second clause names only unbelief as the ground of condemnation.

The signs of verses 17 and 18 are the hardest. The text states that signs 'will accompany those who believe,' but it does not say that every believer will do every one of them, or that a believer is to test God by seeking them. Acts shows demons driven out, Acts 16:18, tongues, Acts 2:4, a viper shaken off without harm, Acts 28:3-6, and the sick healed, Acts 28:8. None of those accounts is a deliberate test of God. Because these verses are also the ones whose place in the earliest text is in question, many Christians choose not to build doctrine or practice on them alone. Nothing in the rest of Scripture tells believers to handle snakes or drink poison to prove their faith, and Jesus Himself refused to put God to the test, Matthew 4:7.

debates.question: How should we read the ending of Mark, and what about verses 9 to 20?

views.label: Mark meant to end at verse 8
views.case: The oldest manuscripts end there, and a deliberately open ending suits the Gospel's themes of fear, failure and the reader's response. Ending on a sentence that closes with 'for' is odd Greek but not impossible, and the ending leaves the reader with the angel's words as the last authoritative voice.

views.label: The original ending was lost
views.case: Some argue that a book would not stop with 'for,' and that the last part of the scroll or the codex was damaged early. The longer ending, on this view, was written to fill the hole, and the short ending is another attempt to do so.

views.label: The longer ending is original, or at least inspired and received
views.case: A minority argue that Mark wrote the longer ending, noting that most manuscripts have it and that Irenaeus appears to know it. Others, while granting it was added, hold that the church has received it as canonical Scripture and that its main teachings, the appearances, the commission and the ascension, are supported by other texts.

debates.bearing: Whatever view is taken, nothing that matters for the Christian faith depends on verses 9 to 20 alone. The resurrection, the commission and the ascension are taught elsewhere, in Matthew 28, Luke 24, John 20 and Acts 1, and a careful reader should say plainly which verses are in doubt.

debates.question: What are the signs of verses 17 and 18 meant to do?

views.label: They are for all believers in every age
views.case: The verse says the signs 'will accompany those who believe,' with no limit of time, so some hold that these gifts are available to the church today, and that the church should expect and ask for them.

views.label: They belonged to the apostolic age
views.case: Others note that Hebrews 2:3-4 describes signs as a confirmation of the message of those who first heard it, and that verse 20 says the Lord confirmed 'His word by the signs that accompanied it.' On this view the signs authenticated the first preaching and are not a standing requirement.

views.label: They are a promise of the kingdom's power, not a test
views.case: A third view treats the verses as a general promise that the gospel will go forward with the Lord's power, which He gives as He wills, Hebrews 2:4, without making any single sign, especially snakes and poison, a measure of faith.

debates.bearing: All sides can agree that the verses never make signs the ground of salvation, and that the Lord, not the believer, decides when and how He acts. Using these verses to demand dangerous demonstrations goes against the way Jesus Himself refused to test God.

study.originalLanguages:
The young man's message turns on a verb form. 'You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified,' verse 6, uses a perfect participle, estauromenon, in Greek, the one who has been crucified and stands as the crucified one. The tense says that the cross is not erased. He is risen, yet He remains the one who was nailed there. The next clause, 'He has risen,' uses the passive form of the verb for raising, which Scripture regularly uses when God is the actor. Mark does not say Jesus 'rose' here; he says He 'was raised,' by the Father.

Mark uses two strong words for the women's state. The young man tells them not to be 'alarmed,' from ekthambeo, a rare word for a startled, shuddering amazement. Mark has used the same verb of the crowd's astonishment when Jesus came down from the mountain, Mark 9:15, and of Jesus' own distress in Gethsemane, Mark 14:33. In verse 8 they flee with tromos kai ekstasis, 'trembling and bewilderment,' and the second word, ekstasis, is the one Mark used of those who saw Jairus' daughter raised, Mark 5:42. The same word covers both astonishment at a miracle and being beside oneself.

The promise 'He is going ahead of you,' verse 7, uses proago, to lead the way. It is the verb of Mark 14:28 ('I will go ahead of you into Galilee') and the verb of Mark 10:32, where on the road to Jerusalem 'Jesus was walking ahead of them' while the followers were afraid. A shepherd goes before his flock. Mark's whole journey was Jesus in front, the disciples behind, and the resurrection does not change the order.

In verse 14 the Lord rebukes the Eleven for 'hardness of heart,' sklerokardia, the word Jesus used of Israel's stubbornness over divorce in Mark 10:5. Mark has used a near relation of it of the disciples before, in Mark 6:52 and 8:17, when 'their hearts had been hardened.' The disciples' persistent blindness now becomes the occasion of a rebuke, and the next words are a commission.

The commission itself is kerysso, 'to herald,' and the audience is pase te ktisei, 'all creation,' which the BSB renders 'every creature.' Paul uses very similar wording in Colossians 1:23. The gospel is meant to be proclaimed as a king's herald proclaims an event, not offered as an opinion.

The ascension verb in verse 19, 'taken up,' is a form of analambano, the verb used in the Greek Old Testament for Elijah being taken up into heaven in 2 Kings 2:11, and used of Jesus in Acts 1:2. But Elijah is carried away and not seen again. The verse then goes on to say that Jesus 'sat down at the right hand of God,' which is the language of Psalm 110:1. He does not merely disappear; He takes a seat, and the seated posture is the mark of a finished work, Hebrews 10:12.

typology.type: Jonah's three days and the sign of the prophet
typology.fulfillment: Jesus said no sign would be given to a wicked generation 'except the sign of the prophet Jonah,' and added, 'As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth,' Matthew 12:39-40. Jonah, thrown into the deep for the sake of the sailors and returning alive, is a picture of a man given up for others and brought back. In Christ the picture is fulfilled in a way Jonah never could: He did not go down by His own disobedience but by obedience, and the one who returns goes on to send His word to the nations, as Jonah did to Nineveh, but with a better and permanent result.

Leviticus 23:10-11 commands Israel to bring a sheaf of firstfruits and have the priest wave it before the LORD 'on the day after the Sabbath.' The first day of the week, verse 2, is that day. Paul calls Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and adds 'each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him,' 15:23. The sheaf was the pledge and first part of the whole harvest. The type reaches its fullness only when the rest of the harvest comes. It falls short in that a sheaf is only a sample, but Christ's rising is also the cause of the rest.

typology.type: Elijah taken up, and the enthroned Lord
typology.fulfillment: Elijah 'went up into heaven in a whirlwind,' 2 Kings 2:11, and the prophets were left to wait for his return, Malachi 4:5. Jesus is also taken up, verse 19, but with a different end. Elijah's departure left an empty place and a mantle; Jesus' departure is an enthronement. He sits at God's right hand, Psalm 110:1, 'far above all rule and authority,' Ephesians 1:20-22. The type falls short because Elijah went up to escape the world; Jesus goes up to rule it, and to send the Spirit, Acts 2:33.

typology.type: Blessing to the families of the earth
typology.fulfillment: The call to Abraham ended with a promise that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3, and the servant of Isaiah is made 'a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth,' Isaiah 49:6. The command to go 'into all the world' in verse 15 is the working out of that promise. In Christ the blessing is no longer held within one nation. It goes to every creature by the proclamation of a risen King, Luke 24:47. The earlier pattern fell short in that Israel mostly kept the blessing at home; the church is sent out.

study.christ:
The chapter shows Christ as the crucified who is alive. The young man does not say 'Jesus of Nazareth is here,' or 'Jesus has escaped.' He says that the one who has been crucified has been raised. The identity of the risen one and the crucified one is the point. Everything Jesus said about the cross is confirmed, because everything He said about the resurrection has proved true. The disciples had held back from asking what He meant by rising from the dead, Mark 9:10, and 9:32. Now they are meant to see that He meant exactly what He said.

He is the Lord who restores. The message names 'His disciples and Peter,' and that specific word is a small act of grace to the man who had insisted 'I never will' fall away and then denied Him with curses, Mark 14:29-31, 14:72. This is the shepherd, struck, now gathering the sheep, as He promised in Mark 14:27-28. He does not wait for the disciples to repent first. He goes ahead and waits for them where He said He would be.

He is the one whose resurrection vindicates His claims. The high priest had asked, 'Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?' and Jesus had answered 'I am,' with the promise that they would see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, Mark 14:61-62. That promise is kept in verse 19: He 'sat down at the right hand of God.' Paul says the resurrection declared Him with power to be the Son of God, Romans 1:4. The cross looked like a refutation; the empty tomb is the answer.

He is the first of a harvest. 'Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The Adam who brought death is answered by the one through whom 'the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man,' 15:21-22. That gives believers a hope beyond comfort: their own dead will be raised, and their lives now are lived in the power of a resurrection already begun, Romans 6:4.

He is the Lord who commissions. In verse 15 the Lord gives the gospel to His people to carry, and in verse 20 He is the one who 'worked through them.' The Gospel that began with the gospel of Jesus Christ, Mark 1:1, now ends with the gospel going out, and Jesus is still the actor in both halves: He is 'the Lord' who works with them from heaven.

A caution applies. The resurrection is not a general picture of spring or renewal. It is an event, tied to a place, 'see the place where they put Him,' and to named witnesses. And the empty tomb is not left to speak for itself, since in Mark it is the word of the angel that explains it and in the other Gospels it is the appearances of Jesus Himself.
study.god:
The chapter shows the Father as the God who raises. The passive 'He has risen,' verse 6, is in Greek 'He has been raised,' and Scripture elsewhere is clear who does the raising: 'God raised Him up on the third day,' Acts 10:40. The Father who gave His Son up in Mark 15 now vindicates Him. The crucifixion and the resurrection are two moments of one purpose, and neither is complete without the other.

God keeps His word across a gap that looked final. Jesus had said, three times and in plain terms, that He would die and rise after three days, and the Gospel has shown that no one understood. The women arrive with spices, the disciples have scattered, and Peter has wept. In the middle of that failure, God does exactly what had been promised. The faithfulness of God does not depend on the understanding or the courage of His people.

God is the stronger power. The stone was 'extremely large,' the guard and the seal belong to another Gospel, and the tomb was a place no one expected to leave. The stone's removal says that the obstacle the women feared has already been dealt with. God does not wait for our solutions before He acts; He often has already moved when we arrive to discuss the problem.

God is gracious to the weak. He does not choose the brave or the quick. He sends the message first to women who flee, to a Peter who had denied, to Eleven who 'did not believe' and who receive a rebuke and a commission in the same breath, verses 14 and 15. The rebuke is real, because God does not excuse unbelief, and the commission is real, because God does not let their unbelief cancel His plan.

God is the God of the whole creation and of the nations. The gospel is to go to 'every creature,' and to 'all the world.' He is not a tribal deity. The God who called Abraham so that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, now sends His people out under the banner of the risen Son.

God reigns through the ascended Christ. The Son sits at His right hand, Psalm 110:1, and from there 'the Lord worked through them, confirming His word,' verse 20. The ascension does not mean God is distant. It means God rules from a throne where a human being now sits, and works on earth through those who carry His word.

For worship, the chapter asks for a hushed and joyful alarm, the sort that the women felt and the sort that the commission turns into witness. The God who raised Jesus is the God who is still going ahead of His people, and who can be trusted to meet us where He has said.

crossReferences.note: 'After I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.' Spoken on the night He was betrayed, this is what the angel recalls in 16:7 with the words 'just as He told you.' The resurrection is not a surprise to Jesus. It is the fulfilment of what He had already said to the very men who would run.

The disciples were forbidden to speak 'until the Son of Man had risen from the dead,' and they spent their time puzzling over what that rising could mean. The empty tomb answers a question they were afraid to ask, and shows how much of Mark's Gospel has been leaning on this morning.

Asked if He is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One, Jesus answers 'I am,' and promises the Son of Man will be seen 'sitting at the right hand of Power.' The seating at God's right hand in 16:19 begins to fulfil that promise, and the court that mocked Him is told what it will see.

'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' Jesus applied it to Himself in Mark 12:36, and Peter does the same in Acts 2:34-35. Verse 19 uses the psalm's picture of the enthroned king, who waits while the enemies are subdued.

Paul's old summary says Christ was buried, raised on the third day, and 'appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve,' and then to more than five hundred. It shows that the church from its earliest years proclaimed the resurrection as a public event with named witnesses, not a private feeling.

Matthew's commission takes place on a mountain in Galilee, the place promised in Mark 16:7. 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me' is the ground of the command, and 'I am with you always' is the promise that matches Mark's 'the Lord worked through them.'

Luke shows the risen Lord insisting on His reality: 'Touch Me and see,' and eating a piece of fish. He also opens the Scriptures to them and says repentance and forgiveness will be preached to all nations. It fills out what Mark 16:14 to 15 summarizes, the rebuke and the sending.

John gives the fullest account of Mary Magdalene's meeting with the risen Jesus, matching Mark 16:9. She does not recognize Him until He says her name. It shows the same combination found in Mark: the first witness is a woman, and the first word is personal.

Luke's second account of the ascension: 'He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight,' and the promise that He will come back in the same way. It confirms that the ascension of Mark 16:19 was a real departure and carries with it the promise of a return.

Salvation 'was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him,' and affirmed by God 'through signs, wonders, various miracles.' This is the best commentary on Mark 16:20, where the Lord works with His witnesses and confirms the word by accompanying signs.

The servant is to be more than the restorer of Israel: 'I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth.' The command to preach to every creature in Mark 16:15 is the carrying of that light by the people of the risen Servant.

Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' and 'in Christ all will be made alive.' It takes the empty tomb of Mark 16 beyond a single event to the first stage of a general resurrection, and so to the believer's own hope.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story began with God speaking life into being and with a man made from dust and breathed into by God. It turned dark with a promise broken in a garden and a word spoken over the man, 'to dust you will return,' Genesis 3:19. From then on every page of the Old Testament carries the weight of that sentence: 'and then he died' is the refrain of Genesis 5, and Israel, like the nations, buries its dead. The long hope that God would one day answer is spoken in small places, in Hosea's 'on the third day He will raise us up,' Hosea 6:2, and in the psalmist's confidence that God would not let His Holy One see decay, Psalm 16:10.

Mark 16 is where that hope breaks into history. The sealed place, the large stone and the burial cloths belong to the story of the curse, and the open tomb is where the curse is first answered. What began in the garden with the serpent's lie, 'You will not surely die,' Genesis 3:4, ends with the tomb empty because the one who bore the curse has overcome it. The first Adam brought death to those in him, and 'the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man,' 1 Corinthians 15:21, the last Adam who is the firstfruits.

The chapter also resolves the question of the Gospel's opening line. The 'beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God,' Mark 1:1, now reaches the end of its first stage. The Son of God was declared with power by the resurrection, Romans 1:4, and has been seated where Psalm 110 said He would be. The nations, promised blessing to Abraham, are now addressed by name: 'every creature.'

Mark's last scene is a sending. The disciples who fled are commissioned, the women who were afraid are given a word, and the church is born into a world where the King is both hidden in heaven and at work through His people. They live between the first rising and the last, between the empty tomb and the day He returns, as the angels said, 'in the same way you have seen Him go,' Acts 1:11.

The end of the story is the new creation in which death itself is undone: 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The tomb outside Jerusalem is the first sign that the one seated on the throne will say, 'Behold, I make all things new,' Revelation 21:5.

quiz.q: What did the women find and hear at the tomb?

options.text: The stone rolled away and a messenger announcing that Jesus the crucified had risen and was not there.
options.note: Mark 16:4-6; the empty tomb and the announcement of the resurrection.

options.text: The body of Jesus still lying where it had been placed.
options.note: The opposite; He was not there, for He had risen.

options.text: An empty tomb, which they could not explain.
options.note: True that the tomb was empty, but it should include the messenger's clear announcement that He had risen.

options.text: Soldiers guarding a sealed tomb.
options.note: Mark records the women finding the stone already rolled away and a messenger, not guards at a sealed tomb.

quiz.q: What is significant about the message, tell His disciples and Peter?

options.text: It shows the risen Jesus' grace toward His failing disciples, singling out Peter who had denied Him.
options.note: Mark 16:7; the personal mention of Peter is tender grace after his denial.

options.text: It shows Peter was the leader who deserved special honour.
options.note: It is grace, not honour earned; Peter had just denied Jesus three times.

options.text: It reveals Jesus' mercy toward those who had failed Him.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should note the specific naming of Peter, who had denied Him.

options.text: It means the other disciples were no longer welcome.
options.note: The message is for all the disciples, with Peter named to reassure him, not to exclude others.

quiz.q: What does the resurrection reveal about Jesus and His work?

options.text: That God raised Him as He foretold, vindicating His crucified Son and defeating death.
options.note: He has risen, God's verdict that the cross accomplished salvation, Mark 8:31.

options.text: That Jesus was a great teacher whose ideas lived on.
options.note: The resurrection is a bodily rising, God's vindication of Jesus, not merely surviving influence.

options.text: That God vindicated Jesus and conquered death through Him.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should note that this fulfilled Jesus' own repeated predictions.

options.text: That the crucifixion had been a mistake now undone.
options.note: The resurrection confirms the cross as God's saving plan, not a mistake.

quiz.q: What does the risen Jesus commission His disciples to do?

options.text: Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.
options.note: Mark 16:15; the mission turns the whole Gospel outward to the world.

options.text: Stay in Jerusalem and wait quietly for His return.
options.note: The commission sends them out into all the world, not into passive waiting.

options.text: Proclaim the good news of His death and resurrection widely.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should include the sweep to all the world and every creature.

options.text: Teach only their own people the law of Moses.
options.note: The commission is to all the world with the gospel, not to their own people alone.

quiz.q: What happened to Jesus after He commissioned His disciples, in the ending as printed?

options.text: He was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God, reigning as Lord.
options.note: Mark 16:19; the ascension and session fulfil Psalm 110:1.

options.text: He remained on earth to lead the disciples in person.
options.note: He ascended to heaven and was seated at God's right hand.

options.text: He ascended to heaven to reign at God's right hand.
options.note: Correct, but it should note that from there He worked with the disciples, confirming His word.

options.text: He disappeared without any further word.
options.note: He ascended visibly after commissioning them, and continued to work through them.

questions: The women came expecting to anoint a dead body and found a risen Lord. Where might God be about to surprise your low expectations with resurrection hope?
The risen Jesus sent word specifically to Peter, who had denied Him. How does His grace to failures like Peter speak to your own failures?
Jesus rebuked the disciples' unbelief in the resurrection reports. Where are you slow to believe what God has clearly promised?
The risen Lord sends His people to preach the gospel to every creature. What part might God be calling you to play in that mission where you are?
Jesus reigns now at God's right hand and works with His witnesses. How does knowing the crucified Jesus is the reigning Lord strengthen you to live and speak for Him?

translationNotes.note: Many of the earliest and most reliable manuscripts end the Gospel here, with the women fleeing in fear. This abrupt ending throws the reader back on Jesus' own promise that He is risen and will be seen in Galilee, and calls for a response of faith.

These verses, the longer ending, are absent from the earliest manuscripts and differ in style from the rest of Mark; some manuscripts have a shorter ending instead. They are printed here as part of the received text, and their content, the appearances, the commission, and the ascension, agrees with the other Gospels and Acts, but distinctive doctrines or practices should not be built on them alone.

The accompanying signs describe the confirming works of the apostolic era; they are not a promise that every believer will handle snakes or drink poison safely, and they must never be turned into a test of faith. Read them in light of the clearer teaching of the whole New Testament.
